opus-5.5.text:
Teleoperation has been incredibly important. It's how most of us got robots to do anything interesting with learning at all. But it has some fundamental limits that I think become more obvious the more you scale it.

The first is just throughput. A human operator is in the loop for every single second of data. You can hire more operators and build more stations, but the cost scales roughly linearly with the data. If you believe, as many of us do, that robot learning will need data on a scale closer to what language models see, linear human cost doesn't get you there.

The second limit is more subtle, and I think more important. Teleoperated data reflects the human's strategy, filtered through an awkward interface. The operator sees through cameras, has limited force feedback, and is controlling a body that isn't theirs. So the demonstrations tend to be slow, cautious, and narrow. You mostly get successful trajectories along a few "safe" paths. The robot rarely sees what happens when things go slightly wrong, or how to recover. Yet that's exactly the situation it ends up in at deployment.

That's where robot-generated experience comes in. Once you have a policy that's reasonably competent, even one bootstrapped from teleop, the robot can start collecting data on its own. It can run autonomously, attempt tasks many times, and generate failures and near-misses naturally. With some form of reward or success signal, whether a learned classifier, a vision-language model judging outcomes, or a human giving sparse feedback rather than full demonstrations, you can turn that experience into improvement. That's essentially reinforcement learning on real hardware, or self-improvement loops.

I think of it as a shift in what the human contributes. Instead of being the hands, the human becomes more of a teacher or supervisor: setting up tasks, resetting occasionally, giving corrections when the robot is stuck. One person can oversee many robots. The data distribution also shifts toward the robot's own behavior, which helps with the mismatch you get when a policy trained on human data drifts into states the human never visited.

There are real challenges, of course. Autonomous collection needs safety, reliable resets, and good reward signals, and none of those are solved. Self-generated data can also reinforce bad habits if you aren't careful about what you learn from. So I don't see it replacing teleoperation outright. Teleop remains the best way to seed new skills and get off the ground. But for scaling and robustness, letting the robot generate its own experience is where much of the leverage will come from. A useful analogy is pretraining followed by RL in language models: demonstrations give you the prior, and the robot's own experience is how it actually gets good.

r001.rationale: It says a competent robot can run autonomously on real hardware and collect its own task experience, including failures and near-misses.

r002.rationale: It describes robots attempting tasks on their own and using that experience to improve a policy initially bootstrapped from teleoperation.

r003.rationale: It says one person can oversee many robots and frames robot-generated experience as the path to scaling data collection beyond teleoperation’s linear human cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me start with what teleoperation is actually good at, because I don't want to sound like I'm dismissing it. Teleop gives you clean, intentional demonstrations. A human puts on a VR rig or grabs a leader arm, and you get trajectories where someone with a working brain decided what to do at every moment. That's incredibly valuable for bootstrapping. Almost every manipulation policy that works today started from that kind of data.

But it has hard limits, and they're structural, not just engineering problems you solve with more money.

The first is scale. A good teleoperator might produce a few hundred useful episodes a day, and you need skilled people, hardware that doesn't break, and a lot of tedious resets. Compare that to language models, which got to ride on the entire internet for free. Robotics has nothing like that. If you want to go from thousands of demos to hundreds of millions, you cannot hire your way there.

The second is coverage. Humans demonstrate the happy path. They almost never show you what happens when the grasp slips, when the drawer sticks, when the object is turned slightly differently from what you expect. So the policy learns the center of the distribution and falls apart at the edges, which is exactly where real deployment lives.

The third is subtler, and it's the one I care about most. Teleop data is about the human's body and the human's perception, filtered through a robot. The operator is compensating for latency, for a bad viewpoint, for the fact that the gripper isn't their hand. You get strategies that are human-shaped, not robot-shaped. The robot might be capable of a better, faster, more reliable way of doing the task that no human would ever demonstrate because it feels unnatural to us.

Robot-generated experience attacks all three of those. The idea is that once you have a baseline policy, you let the robot act, in the real world or in simulation or both, and you treat everything that happens as data. Not just successes. Failures, recoveries, near misses, the weird stuff. The robot is generating its own curriculum.

On scale, this changes the economics completely. A fleet of robots running overnight produces more interaction data than a teleop team produces in a month, and the marginal cost per episode trends toward electricity and wear. On coverage, the robot naturally visits the states that humans skip, because it's imperfect and the world is messy. The failure cases stop being rare. On the embodiment problem, the robot discovers strategies that fit its own body, because it's optimizing for its own outcomes rather than mimicking ours.

Now, I want to be honest about the catch, because it's a big one. Robot experience is only useful if you can say something about whether it went well. Teleop comes with a free label: the human did it, so it probably worked. Autonomous experience doesn't. You need either a reward signal, a success detector, or a way to learn from the data without needing a verdict at all. That's where most of the real difficulty is right now. If your success classifier is wrong ten percent of the time, you are training on ten percent poison, and the policy will happily learn to exploit the classifier instead of doing the task.

So the way I think about it is as a flywheel rather than a replacement. Teleop gets you off the ground and anchors the behavior in something sensible. Then the robot generates experience, you filter it with whatever judgment you can muster, including from vision-language models, from physical outcomes, from humans doing cheap review instead of expensive demonstration, and you fold it back in. Each loop makes the policy more robust, which makes the next round of autonomous data better, which makes the filter easier. Humans move up the stack, from doing the task to supervising the task to just occasionally auditing.

And the long-term bet is that this is the only path that compounds. Human demonstration is linear in human effort. Robot experience is linear in robots, and robots are the thing we're trying to make cheap in the first place. The field that figures out how to make that loop stable, where the data the robot produces reliably makes the robot better rather than drifting into nonsense, that's the field that gets its version of the internet-scale moment. We're not there yet, but I think that's where the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot acts in the real world or simulation and treats what happens as data, including failures and recoveries.

r002.rationale: It describes teleoperation as the starting point, then says the robot generates its own experience in a compounding flywheel that makes the policy more robust.

r003.rationale: It says a fleet running overnight can produce more interaction data than a teleoperation team does in a month, and argues that scaling with robots addresses the data bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that teleoperation ties data collection to human time. If you want twice as much experience, you generally need more operators or more hours. It’s useful for teaching a robot what a task looks like, but it’s hard to cover all the situations the robot might encounter.

Robot-generated experience can change that. Once the robot has a basic capability, it can attempt tasks, observe what happens, and use those outcomes to improve. It can also encounter failures and practice recovery—things a human operator might naturally avoid or correct before they become part of the data.

But generating more experience isn’t enough by itself. You need a reliable way to judge whether the robot succeeded, and you need exploration to be safe and informative. Otherwise, you can collect a huge amount of repetitive or unhelpful data.

So I see the two as complementary: human demonstrations give the robot a starting point, and autonomous experience lets it expand beyond what people can explicitly demonstrate. The important step is closing that loop between trying, evaluating, and learning.

r001.rationale: It says robots can attempt tasks, observe outcomes, and learn from autonomous experience, presenting robot activity as a source of experience beyond teleoperation.

r002.rationale: It says autonomous experience lets robots expand beyond what people explicitly demonstrate by attempting tasks and observing what happens.

r003.rationale: It does not mention data from large numbers of deployed robots or suggest that such scale could overcome current data availability concerns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that teleoperation can give robots a starting point, but it’s hard to make it the entire learning process. Every demonstration takes human time, and you only collect the situations that someone actually encounters or chooses to demonstrate. As tasks become more varied, that becomes a bottleneck.

Robot-generated experience can expand that process. A robot tries a task, observes the result, and uses that feedback to improve. Failures become useful data, and you can collect experience in situations where the current policy is weak rather than simply collecting more demonstrations.

But generating experience isn’t enough by itself. You need a reliable way to judge whether the robot succeeded, and you need to keep exploration safe. Otherwise, you can generate a lot of data without learning very much. So I see the two as complementary: human demonstrations establish useful behavior, and autonomous experience lets the robot practice, discover mistakes, and improve beyond what people explicitly showed it.

r001.rationale: The response says robots can try tasks, observe results, and use that feedback as experience, presenting autonomous practice as a source of data beyond human demonstrations.

r002.rationale: It describes demonstrations as establishing useful behavior, then says autonomous experience lets robots practice and improve beyond what people explicitly showed them.

r003.rationale: The response says robot-generated experience can expand data collection, but does not mention large numbers of deployed robots or say that their data could eventually resolve data-availability concerns.
